defaults.permitted_development: A wraparound extension is not a separate permitted development category. It only avoids planning permission where every rear and side element fits the Class A householder rules together; many true wraparound layouts do not.

rules.height_rules: The side element should stay single storey and within the normal 4m height cap, with eaves no higher than the existing house and no more than 3m within 2m of a boundary.
rules.depth_rules: The rear element should stay within the Class A rear projection limits measured from the original rear wall, while the side element should remain no more than half the width of the original house.
rules.boundary_rules: No part should be forward of the principal elevation or a side elevation facing a highway, and designated-land side elements usually need permission.
rules.roof_rules: The roof should remain subordinate and should not introduce excluded features such as balconies, verandas or raised platforms.
rules.materials_rules: Exterior materials should be similar in appearance to the existing house so the combined rear-and-side form still reads as part of the dwelling.

height_rules.title: Height Limits for a Wraparound Form
height_rules.intro: A wraparound extension is often tested by the side-extension height rules first, because that flank element is the restrictive part.
rules: The side element should remain single storey.
Overall height should not exceed 4m where relying on the normal householder side-extension route.
Eaves should not be higher than the existing house eaves.
If the extension comes within 2m of a boundary, the eaves should not exceed 3m.
height_rules.details: Although people often describe these schemes as one project, planning law does not create a special wraparound class. The side element still has to satisfy the normal side-extension rules under Class A. That usually means keeping it single storey and within the standard height limits. A design that works comfortably as a rear extension can still fail once the side return and its roof form are added.
height_rules.exceptions: If the side element becomes too tall or starts to introduce upper-floor accommodation, planning permission will normally be required.

depth_rules.title: Rear Projection and Side Width Tests
depth_rules.intro: A wraparound layout has to pass both the rear-extension and side-extension size tests together.
rules: The rear element should stay within the normal rear projection limits measured from the original rear wall.
The side element should be no more than half the width of the original house.
Earlier additions can reduce how much enlargement remains available.
A larger home extension prior approval route does not solve every side-return issue.
depth_rules.details: The rear part of a wraparound extension is judged against the same rear projection rules used for other Class A extensions, while the side part is judged against the side-extension width rule. That combined test is why many full wraparound schemes end up needing planning permission even where each idea sounds modest on its own. The measurements are taken from the original house, not from a later rear projection or lean-to.
depth_rules.exceptions: If either the rear projection or the side-width test is exceeded, the wraparound scheme will usually need planning permission.

boundary_rules.title: Boundaries, Highways and Designated Land
boundary_rules.intro: Plot position is often the main reason a wraparound extension needs a formal application.
rules: No part should project forward of the principal elevation.
No part should project forward of a side elevation facing a highway.
On Article 2(3) designated land, the side element will usually need planning permission.
Boundary proximity still matters because of the 3m eaves rule within 2m of the boundary.
boundary_rules.details: Because a wraparound extension includes a side return, it inherits the same frontage and highway-facing restrictions as a side extension. Corner plots and visually open flank elevations are therefore much harder to keep within permitted development. On designated land, the side element is usually enough on its own to move the project into the planning-application route.
boundary_rules.exceptions: Properties on corner plots, in conservation areas or on other designated land often need permission for wraparound forms even where the rear element looks acceptable.

roof_rules.title: Roof Design on a Wraparound Extension
roof_rules.intro: The roof has to hold the rear and side elements together without creating excluded or over-dominant features.
rules: The combined roof should remain subordinate to the original house.
Balconies, verandas and raised platforms are not included in Class A.
A side-return roof that creates first-floor accommodation will usually need permission.
Complicated roof forms can make a wraparound scheme look larger than its footprint suggests.
roof_rules.details: Wraparound extensions often fail on design rather than pure measurements. A simple single-storey roof form is usually the safest option if permitted development is the goal. Once the proposal starts to create an occupiable upper element, an external platform or a visually dominant side roof, it usually falls outside the Class A householder route.
roof_rules.exceptions: Terraces, high parapets, bulky lantern combinations and upper-level side-return accommodation will normally require planning permission.

materials_rules.title: External Materials and Readability
materials_rules.intro: The bigger the combined side-and-rear form, the more important it is that the finish still looks tied to the host house.
rules: Use exterior materials similar in appearance to the existing house.
The side and rear elevations should feel like one coherent addition.
A strong contrast across a large wraparound footprint can make the extension feel more dominant.
Simple detailing usually works better than multiple competing finishes.
materials_rules.details: The Class A materials condition still applies where the project is being treated as permitted development. Matching or closely related materials help a wraparound addition feel like an integrated enlargement rather than a pieced-together structure. Because these schemes are often visually bigger than a standard rear extension, weak material choices tend to show up more clearly.
materials_rules.exceptions: Heritage settings and listed buildings may need a closer match and often a different consent route altogether.

restrictions.conservation_area: Wraparound extensions often need a full planning application in conservation areas because the side and rear elements can change the reading of the original house from several viewpoints.
restrictions.listed_building: A listed building will usually need listed building consent for works affecting its character, and wraparound schemes often raise both planning and heritage issues together.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions can remove normal householder permitted development rights on selected streets, estates or heritage areas, so the exact designation should be checked before relying on Class A.
